passage: The power had gone in the whole colony, so the evening match between Neem Street and Pipe Lane was the only thing happening, lit by the last of the sunset. When the Pipe Lane children arrived with their plastic bat, Salma folded her arms. 'We're not playing with them. They're dirty. They're like wild animals, they bite.' A few Neem Street kids giggled. Elizabeth Aunty, sitting out on her steps in the heat, called Salma over. 'Which one bites?' Salma pointed vaguely. 'All of them.' 'What's that girl's name, the one with the red clip?' 'I don't know.' 'Then how do you know she bites?' Salma had no answer. The girl with the red clip was holding the ball, waiting. 'Her name is Ruksana,' Elizabeth Aunty said. 'She brings my newspaper. Go and ask if she wants to bowl first.'

qa.q: What was the girl with the red clip holding?
qa.a: The girl with the red clip was holding the ball.

qa.q: Why does calling the Pipe Lane children 'wild animals' make refusing them feel okay to Salma?
qa.a: Seeing them as animals rather than children with names makes shutting them out feel reasonable, so Salma feels justified rather than guilty about being unkind.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth Aunty do that began to change things?
qa.a: She asked for one child's name and then gave it, Ruksana, turning 'all of them' into a real girl, and suggested asking her to bowl first.

qa.q: How might Ruksana feel standing with the ball, waiting?
qa.a: Ruksana might feel unsure and hurt, hearing her lane called dirty and wild when she only wanted to play.

grounding: Shows a child who calls children from a rival lane dirty wild animals and refuses to play, until a neighbour gives one of them a name.

passage: Behind Kunal's building in Baner a new tower was going up, and the workers' children played in the sand beside it. When their ball rolled into the society garden, Kunal kicked it back over the fence, hard. 'Don't touch it, it's filthy,' he told his friends. 'Those kids are like street dogs. They'll steal your cycle.' His cousin Samir, visiting for the weekend, raised an eyebrow. 'Street dogs? The small one just said thank you in Marathi.' Kunal shrugged. 'They're all the same.' 'Have you talked to any of them?' 'Why would I?' Samir walked to the fence. The small boy was there again, holding the ball carefully. 'What's your name?' 'Babu.' 'Kunal, this is Babu. He's seven. Babu, want to play?' Kunal stood very still, his face going red.

qa.q: What is the small boy's name?
qa.a: The small boy's name is Babu.

qa.q: Why does calling them 'street dogs' make it easier for Kunal to kick the ball hard?
qa.a: Kunal feels contempt for them, and seeing them as animals rather than children like himself makes treating them roughly seem normal.

qa.q: What made Samir's approach effective?
qa.a: Samir asked a real question and then introduced one child by name and age, which turned 'those kids' into Babu and made Kunal's words hard to keep saying.

qa.q: What was it like for Babu when the ball was kicked back so hard?
qa.a: Babu still said thank you in Marathi, so he may have felt confused or hurt by the roughness but kept being polite.

grounding: Shows a child who calls construction workers' children filthy street dogs, until a cousin introduces one boy by name.

passage:
'Api, I'm not going to the Eid fair if the Tank Road boys are coming.'
'Why?'
'They're wild. Like jungle animals. They don't even wash.'
Afreen put down her book. 'Who told you that?'
'Everyone knows. Faizan says.'
'Do you know any of them?'
'No. They're just... Tank Road.'
'Remember the boy who found your cap when it blew into the drain last Eid? Brought it back and wouldn't take the ten rupees?'
Zubin frowned. 'Yeah.'
'Imran. He lives on Tank Road.'
'He does?'
'Mm-hm. Was he a jungle animal?'
Zubin picked at the sofa cushion. 'No. He was nice.'
'So maybe "the Tank Road boys" is really Imran, and some other boys with names.'
Zubin was quiet for a while. 'Can I wear my cap to the fair?' he asked at last.

qa.q: What did Imran find last Eid?
qa.a: Imran found Zubin's cap when it blew into the drain.

qa.q: Why does Zubin feel sure the Tank Road boys are 'wild'?
qa.a: Zubin is wary of boys he has never met, and having heard it from Faizan and 'everyone', the label feels like fact and staying away seems right.

qa.q: Which reminder from Afreen was the turning point?
qa.a: Reminding Zubin that Imran, the boy who returned the cap, lives on Tank Road gave the group a real face and name, which broke the 'jungle animals' picture.

qa.q: How might Imran feel if he heard Tank Road boys called jungle animals?
qa.a: Imran would likely feel hurt and unfairly judged, especially after going out of his way to return Zubin's cap.

grounding: Shows a child who calls boys from another road wild jungle animals and refuses to go to a fair, until his sister names one of them.

passage:
I'm Jagdish, and last summer in our railway colony I had a rule: no playing with the Line kids. They lived in the huts by the tracks, and I told everyone they were jungli and dirty. So when their ball bounced into our lane, I kicked it into the drain. 'They're used to muck,' I said. 'They won't mind.'
My cousin Preeti fished it out and walked it back to them. I was angry with her.
The next day I saw a girl from the huts, Sulochana, crying by the drain and washing that ball with her hands. It was her birthday ball, Preeti told me.
I didn't feel like a winner. I felt small.
Now I say their names. Sulochana bowls better than me.

qa.q: What did Jagdish do with the ball when it bounced into the lane?
qa.a: Jagdish kicked it into the drain.

qa.q: Why did kicking the ball away feel okay to Jagdish at that moment?
qa.a: Jagdish had been calling the Line kids jungli and dirty, so they seemed not to feel things the same way; 'they won't mind' made the unkind act feel harmless.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Jagdish, and what changed after it?
qa.a: Seeing Sulochana crying and washing her birthday ball; Jagdish felt small, dropped the 'jungli' label and started using the children's names.

qa.q: How might Preeti have seen the Line kids differently from Jagdish?
qa.a: Preeti treated them as ordinary children whose ball mattered, so she fished it out and took it back; to her they were simply neighbours.

grounding: A child who calls the children from the huts dirty and wild treats their things roughly, until seeing one girl's tears makes her a person again.

passage:
Coach's note, Saturday junior football, Old City ground. Noor.
Hafsa (9) refused to join a mixed team today. 'Not with the Kaman Gali lot. They're wild. They bite.' When I paired her with Mehrunnisa from that lane, Hafsa pulled the yellow bib off Mehrunnisa's shoulders and said, 'She doesn't need it, they play like goats anyway.' Two of her friends laughed.
I stopped the drill. I didn't lecture. I asked each child to tell the group one thing about their partner. Mehrunnisa said Hafsa has the fastest left foot on the ground. Hafsa went quiet and then said, very low, 'Mehrunnisa keeps goal for her brother's team.'
Next week: keep the pairs mixed across lanes, and give Hafsa and Mehrunnisa the passing drill together.

qa.q: What did Hafsa pull off Mehrunnisa's shoulders?
qa.a: The yellow bib.

qa.q: Why did grabbing the bib seem acceptable to Hafsa?
qa.a: Hafsa had already decided the Kaman Gali children were 'wild' and played 'like goats', so treating Mehrunnisa roughly did not feel like hurting a real person.

qa.q: What choice did Coach Noor make after stopping the drill, and why did it help?
qa.a: Noor chose not to lecture but had each child say one thing about their partner; hearing Mehrunnisa praise her left foot led Hafsa to see and name a real person.

qa.q: What might the afternoon have felt like for Mehrunnisa?
qa.a: Mehrunnisa was called a goat and had her bib pulled off in front of others, which likely stung, yet she still said something generous about Hafsa.

grounding: A coach notes a child who calls children from another lane wild and treats one roughly, and helps her see one of them as a person.

passage: In Nabha, the children of Mandi Lane never played with the children from across the canal. 'They're jungli,' Rehana told her little cousin, repeating what the older kids said. 'Dirty. They bite like dogs.' On Sunday the ball rolled over the canal bridge, and a girl from the other side, Gurleen, picked it up and held it out. Rehana snatched it and ran. 'Don't touch her, she's full of germs,' she shouted, and her friends laughed and threw pebbles at the bridge. Gurleen stood there, her hand still out. That evening Rehana's Nani, who had watched from the roof, called her up. 'What's that girl's name?' Rehana shrugged. 'One of them.' 'Go and find out tomorrow,' Nani said. 'You don't throw stones at someone whose name you know.'

qa.q: What did Rehana's friends throw at the bridge?
qa.a: They threw pebbles at the bridge.

qa.q: Why was it easy for Rehana to snatch the ball and shout about germs?
qa.a: Calling the other children dirty and like dogs made them feel less like real children, so being rough didn't make Rehana feel guilty in the moment.

qa.q: Why is Nani's instruction to find out the girl's name wise?
qa.a: Learning Gurleen's name turns 'one of them' back into a person, which makes cruelty much harder.

qa.q: What was the moment on the bridge like for Gurleen?
qa.a: Gurleen was trying to be kind by returning the ball and was shouted at and pelted instead, left standing with her hand still out.

grounding: A child calls children from across the canal dirty and like dogs, which makes throwing pebbles and refusing to play seem acceptable.

passage: On Adeyemi Street in Lagos, the boys played football every evening in the gap between the parked cars. Emeka was the best dribbler, and he made the rules. 'Nobody from Harbour Road,' he said when Daniel from the next street came to watch. 'They're like wild animals over there. They kick your legs and steal the ball.' The other boys nodded. Daniel sat on the kerb for three evenings, watching. On the fourth, the ball flew over a wall into a compound. Daniel climbed up, dropped over, threw it back, and walked home without a word. Emeka's mother had seen it all from the balcony. At dinner she asked, 'Which wild animal gave you the ball back?' Emeka ate his rice and didn't answer. The next evening, he told Daniel he could play in goal.

qa.q: Where did the boys play football?
qa.a: They played in the gap between the parked cars on Adeyemi Street.

qa.q: Why did Emeka call the Harbour Road boys wild animals?
qa.a: The label let him see them as a group to keep out rather than as boys like him, so he felt no guilt or sympathy while excluding Daniel.

qa.q: What helped Emeka change his mind?
qa.a: Seeing Daniel return the ball, and his mother's question, made him face one real, kind person instead of a label.

qa.q: What were those three evenings like for Daniel?
qa.a: Daniel sat on the kerb watching, left out and probably lonely, yet he still helped when the ball was lost.

grounding: A child calls boys from a rival street wild animals and refuses to let them play, until one kind act and a parent's question bring back a face.

passage: In the school hostel, the girls of Block A had decided that the Block C girls, who came from the hill villages, were 'like goats'. 'They smell,' Aparna whispered at dinner, 'and they eat like animals.' When the dining hall filled up and two Block C girls sat at her table, Aparna picked up her plate and moved, and her friends followed, giggling. The two girls sat alone at a table for eight. Mahima Ma'am, the house mother, had seen it. After dinner she called Aparna to the common room. 'The girl in the blue sweater. What's her name?' Aparna didn't know. 'Dolkar. She's in your maths class. She won the handwriting prize. She's homesick, like you were in June.' Aparna looked at the floor. 'Tomorrow at lunch,' Ma'am said, 'you'll sit with her and ask her one thing about her village.'

qa.q: What prize did Dolkar win?
qa.a: Dolkar won the handwriting prize.

qa.q: Why did Aparna move tables?
qa.a: Seeing the Block C girls as 'like goats' let Aparna feel disgust instead of guilt, so leaving them alone felt acceptable.

qa.q: What did Mahima Ma'am do to restore empathy?
qa.a: She gave Dolkar a name and a story, maths class, a prize, homesickness, and asked Aparna to sit with her and ask about her village.

qa.q: How might Dolkar and her friend feel at the empty table for eight?
qa.a: They would likely feel humiliated and lonely, already homesick and now shunned in front of everyone.

grounding: A child in a hostel calls girls from another block animals and moves tables to avoid them, until the house mother gives one of them a name.

passage:
Monday: Kunal and his brother came from Gali No. 4 with a cricket ball. Baljeet folded his arms. “Not with them. They're dirty. They live like jungli animals over there.” The others laughed, and Kunal left.
Wednesday: The Gali No. 4 kids' ball rolled into Baljeet's lane. Baljeet kicked it into the drain. “They're wild anyway, they won't care.” Nobody stopped him. It felt easy, almost funny.
Saturday: The lane flooded after rain. Baljeet's little sister Simran slipped near the drain and her chappal floated off. It was Kunal who waded in, fished it out and gave it back, then quietly wiped her knee with his sleeve.
Baljeet stood very still. Kunal's hands were muddy, just like his own. He did not look wild at all. Baljeet mumbled, “Thanks,” and couldn't meet his eyes.

qa.q: Where did Baljeet kick the ball on Wednesday?
qa.a: He kicked the Gali No. 4 kids' ball into the drain.

qa.q: Why did kicking the ball feel easy to Baljeet on Wednesday?
qa.a: Calling the children wild made him feel their feelings didn't count, so being rough felt almost funny instead of mean.

qa.q: What could Baljeet do next time he sees Kunal?
qa.a: He could invite Kunal to play cricket and say sorry about the ball, getting to know him as a person rather than as “Gali No. 4”.

qa.q: How might Kunal see Baljeet's lane after Monday and Wednesday?
qa.a: Kunal probably felt insulted and unwelcome there, yet he still helped Simran, which shows he did not answer cruelty with cruelty.

grounding: The beats show a child calling children from another lane dirty and wild, which makes rough treatment feel acceptable until he sees one of them as a person.

passage:
Sahil, you called those boys from the railway quarters “rats” at dinner. Let me, your Karthik mama, tell you where that word took me once.
When I was nine, in Kollam, we lived near the fishermen's colony. We called their children “smelly crabs.” We wouldn't let them near our temple ground to play. One day my friends threw sand in a small boy's eyes and I laughed. Crabs, after all. Who cares what a crab feels?
That boy was Sebastian. Years later, in college, he was the one who stayed up all night with me when my father was in hospital. He never mentioned the sand. I did, finally, and cried saying sorry.
I had made him a crab so I didn't have to see him. Once I saw him, I couldn't unsee it.

qa.q: What did the children call the boys from the fishermen's colony?
qa.a: They called them “smelly crabs” and wouldn't let them play on the temple ground.

qa.q: Why did young Karthik laugh when sand was thrown in the boy's eyes?
qa.a: Calling the boy a crab made his pain seem unreal, so Karthik felt no guilt at the time and laughing felt harmless.

qa.q: At what moment in the story could young Karthik have chosen differently?
qa.a: When his friends threw sand, he could have stopped laughing, helped the boy and refused to use the word crabs again.

qa.q: How might Sebastian have felt about the sand when Karthik finally apologised?
qa.a: Sebastian had likely been hurt long ago but may have felt respected and understood when Karthik named it and said sorry.

grounding: The uncle's memory shows children labelling another group as animals, which made rough treatment feel acceptable.

passage:
The power had gone at five, and the whole society poured downstairs to escape the heat. There was only one lit patch, under the generator lamp near Tower B.
Baljeet and the other kids from Tower D came with a tennis ball.
Ojas stood in the middle of the lit patch. “No D-wing kids. You lot are wild, you break everything, you're like monkeys.” His friends nodded.
Baljeet said, “There's no other light.”
“Not our problem,” Ojas said, and bounced the ball hard off Baljeet's shoulder. It stung. The D-wing kids went and sat in the dark near the gate.
Ojas's mother had seen the ball hit. She came over and said, calmly, “Would you bounce a ball off Baljeet's shoulder if you didn't call him a monkey first?”
Ojas started to answer, then couldn't. The word had made it feel allowed.

qa.q: Where was the only lit patch during the power cut?
qa.a: It was under the generator lamp near Tower B.

qa.q: Why did bouncing the ball off Baljeet's shoulder feel allowed to Ojas?
qa.a: Calling the D-wing kids wild monkeys made Ojas feel they didn't count as real children, so hurting them felt less wrong.

qa.q: Which part of the mother's response helped Ojas see it?
qa.a: She stayed calm and asked a question that connected the label to the hurt, letting Ojas see it for himself.

qa.q: What is it like for the D-wing kids to sit in the dark near the gate?
qa.a: They feel rejected and left out, stuck in the heat and the dark while being called monkeys by a neighbour.

grounding: The passage shows a child calling children from another building wild and refusing to share play space, which makes rough treatment feel acceptable.

passage: During Ganesh festival, the Dadar lane had a cricket match every evening. Anand's side played the kids from Chawl No. 3, the lane behind. Today they asked to join. Anand said loudly, "No way. They're dirty. Like wild animals. They'll bite the ball." His friends laughed. The chawl kids went quiet and walked off. Nirmala Aunty, sitting on her steps with a plate of modaks, called him over. "Anand, who is that boy in the blue shirt?" "I don't know. One of them." "His name is Sameer. His mother makes the modaks you ate yesterday. He came first in the drawing contest at the pandal." Anand looked at the boy in the blue shirt. He didn't look wild. He looked sad. "I didn't know his name," Anand said. "That's easy to fix," said Aunty. Anand walked over slowly. "Sameer? You can bat first."

qa.q: Who made the modaks Anand ate yesterday?
qa.a: Sameer's mother made them.

qa.q: Why did calling the chawl kids animals make it easier for Anand to shut them out?
qa.a: Seeing them as dirty and wild, not as people with names, made refusing them feel fair and stopped Anand feeling guilty.

qa.q: What did Nirmala Aunty do that helped Anand?
qa.a: She gave Anand a name and real details about one boy, which turned "them" into Sameer.

qa.q: How might Sameer have felt walking off after Anand's words?
qa.a: Sameer likely felt hurt and humiliated at being called dirty and wild in front of everyone.

grounding: During a festival a boy calls children from another lane wild animals and refuses to play, until a neighbour gives one of them a name and a story.

passage:
"Zeenat, why won't you let the canal colony kids join the Christmas carol group?"
"Because they're wild, Hrithik. Like animals. They push, they shout."
"All of them?"
"Everyone says so."
"Have you met any?"
"Why would I?"
"Well. I live in the canal colony."
Zeenat stared at him. "You do not."
"Third lane. Blue gate. My mother sews for your Ammi."
"But you're... normal."
"So are they. Rinku does the best voices. Tina can sing higher than anyone in our school."
Zeenat looked at her song sheet. "I didn't mean you."
"You said all of them."
"I just thought..."
"You didn't think about any of them. That's the problem."
Zeenat was quiet for a long time. Then she said, "Does Tina really sing that high?"
"Come and hear her tomorrow."

qa.q: Where does Hrithik live?
qa.a: In the canal colony, third lane, blue gate.

qa.q: Why was Zeenat so sure the canal colony kids were wild?
qa.a: Zeenat had never met any of them, and calling them animals made keeping them out feel reasonable without thinking of real children.

qa.q: What changed Zeenat's mind a little?
qa.a: Learning that Hrithik lived there and hearing about Rinku and Tina gave the group real faces and names.

qa.q: What might Hrithik feel when Zeenat says "you're normal"?
qa.a: Hrithik probably felt hurt and a bit angry that his neighbours were being called animals.

grounding: In a festival carol group a girl calls children from another colony animals and refuses them, until a friend from there gives them faces.

passage:
The summer I was nine, my friends and I had a name for the kids from the back lane behind our building. We called them "the jungli gang". Wild, dirty, like monkeys. We wouldn't play with them. If they came near our cricket, we'd shout them away. I shouted the loudest.
One afternoon in May, my new kite got stuck on the water tank of their building. I stood there crying. A girl from the back lane climbed up the pipe, untangled it, and handed it back to me with both hands. "It's a nice kite," she said. Her name was Zainab. She had a gap in her teeth and laughed at her own jokes.
That evening I felt strange. The word "jungli" didn't fit her at all. It had never fitted anyone. It just made it easier to be mean.
— Mridul

qa.q: Where did Mridul's new kite get stuck?
qa.a: On the water tank of the back-lane building.

qa.q: Why did the name "jungli gang" make shouting at the back-lane kids feel okay?
qa.a: Calling them wild and like monkeys let Mridul feel superior and free of guilt, since they no longer seemed like real children, so being rough felt acceptable.

qa.q: What went wrong in how Mridul's friends treated the back lane, and what could fix it?
qa.a: They judged a whole group by a mean name without knowing anyone; learning names and playing together could fix it.

qa.q: How might Zainab have felt handing the kite back to someone who shouted at her friends?
qa.a: Zainab may have felt a mix of kindness and wariness, choosing to help despite how the back-lane kids were treated.

grounding: An adult recalls calling back-lane children wild and refusing to play with them, until one girl's kindness gave the group a face.

passage:
Summer reading camp, Ward 12 library: volunteer's note, Day 6.
Too hot outside, so I paired the children for a board game. When I paired Zainab with Salma from Kasai Gali, Zainab pushed her chair back. "Not with her. Those Kasai Gali kids are dirty. They're like wild dogs." Salma went very still and stared at the board.
I didn't argue in front of everyone. I asked Zainab to help me carry the water jug, and on the way I asked, "What's Salma's favourite game?" She didn't know. "Then find out one thing about her first."
Back at the table, Salma said ludo, and taught Zainab a new rule. They played two rounds. Tomorrow I will mix the street groups for every activity and speak to both families.

qa.q: What did Zainab say when she was paired with Salma?
qa.a: "Not with her. Those Kasai Gali kids are dirty. They're like wild dogs."

qa.q: Why might calling Salma's street "wild" feel right to Zainab?
qa.a: Zainab seems wary and a bit superior; if the Kasai Gali children are "wild", pushing away feels fair, and Zainab doesn't have to feel bad about hurting anyone.

qa.q: What did the volunteer do that helped?
qa.a: The volunteer avoided a public scolding, asked Zainab privately about Salma's favourite game, and got the two to learn something real about each other, with mixed groups and family talks planned next.

qa.q: What was that moment like for Salma?
qa.a: Salma went very still and stared at the board, so being called dirty and wild probably felt humiliating and hurtful.

grounding: A child calls children from another street dirty and wild and refuses to play, and a volunteer helps her see one real person.
